title: Lesson 1: Preface and Setup
text:
What This Guide Is
Single-cell RNA-seq analysis is often described as a sequence of steps:
QC → normalization → PCA or UMAP → clustering → markers → annotation
Most confusion does not come from running those steps. It comes from interpreting what they mean and what they do not mean.
This free guide is designed to build disciplined reasoning.
You will learn to:
crumbs: 2  Lesson 1: Preface and Setup

title: Lesson 1: Preface and Setup
text:
Understand the data objects (counts and metadata)
Apply QC with explicit thresholds and tradeoffs
Interpret embeddings and clusters carefully
Treat marker-based labels as hypotheses, not conclusions
Translate results into calibrated biological claims
crumbs: 2  Lesson 1: Preface and Setup

title: Lesson 1: Preface and Setup
text:
What This Guide Is Not
This guide is not:

A benchmark of tools
A promise that clustering equals cell types
A replacement for replication and validation

It is a structured foundation that makes downstream choices easier to defend.
crumbs: 2  Lesson 1: Preface and Setup

title: Lesson 1: Preface and Setup
text:
The Reasoning Chain
We follow a reasoning chain that mirrors how interpretation should happen in practice:
Data structure → QC metrics → normalization choices → structure (PCA or UMAP) → clustering → marker evidence → calibrated claim
Each lesson adds one layer. Later layers do not override earlier ones.

title: Lesson 1: Preface and Setup
text:
Interpretation Discipline
Single-cell analysis is vulnerable to over-interpretation because:

Cells are not independent biological replicates
Clusters are algorithmic groupings, not ground truth
Marker genes can be shared across states
Batch effects can look like biology

This guide will repeatedly separate:

What the analysis shows
What the analysis suggests
What the analysis cannot prove

That separation is the core skill.

title: Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics

Alignment Check
Counts columns must match metadata cell IDs.

[1] TRUE


If FALSE, alignment must be fixed before proceeding.
crumbs: 3  Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics

title: Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics
text:
Distribution of Total Counts (nCount_RNA)

ggplot(metadata, aes(x = nCount_RNA)) +
  cdi_geom_histogram(bins = 40, colored = TRUE) +
  cdi_scale_histogram_fill() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of total counts per cell",
    subtitle = "Cells with extremely low counts may be poor quality",
    x = "nCount_RNA",
    y = "Number of cells"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()








Improved Interpretation:
Most cells fall within a relatively narrow range of total counts.
There is no cluster of extremely low-count cells, which reduces the likelihood of empty droplets.
A modest right tail exists. This could represent: - Cells with genuinely higher RNA content - Potential doublets (two cells captured together)
At this stage, there is no justification to remove cells purely based on nCount_RNA.
QC thresholds should not be applied simply because they are common in tutorials.
crumbs: 3  Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics

title: Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics
text:
Distribution of Detected Genes (nFeature_RNA)

ggplot(metadata, aes(x = nFeature_RNA)) +
  cdi_geom_histogram(bins = 40, colored = TRUE) +
  cdi_scale_histogram_fill() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of detected genes per cell",
    subtitle = "Low-feature cells are often low quality",
    x = "nFeature_RNA",
    y = "Number of cells"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()








Improved Interpretation:
The distribution is narrow and largely unimodal.
There is no obvious subpopulation of extremely low-feature cells.
This suggests that technical dropout is not dominating the dataset.
Higher-feature cells could reflect: - Larger or more transcriptionally active cells - Doublets - Or specific biological states
Again, no immediate filtering decision is justified.
crumbs: 3  Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics

title: Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics
text:
Mitochondrial Percentage (percent_mt)

ggplot(metadata, aes(x = percent_mt)) +
  cdi_geom_histogram(bins = 40, colored = TRUE) +
  cdi_scale_histogram_fill() +
  labs(
    title = "Mitochondrial percentage per cell",
    subtitle = "High mitochondrial proportion may indicate stressed or dying cells",
    x = "percent_mt",
    y = "Number of cells"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()








Improved Interpretation:
The mitochondrial percentage shows clear bimodality.
One group of cells has low mitochondrial content (~2–4%), while another shows substantially higher values (~14–18%).
This pattern suggests: - Either a stressed cell subpopulation - Or a batch-driven difference
Before filtering, we must check:

Is high percent_mt enriched in one batch?
Does removing these cells remove a biological cluster?
Are these cells coherent in downstream PCA space?

Blindly applying a “5% mitochondrial cutoff” would eliminate an entire subpopulation.
crumbs: 3  Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics

title: Lesson 2: Data Structure and QC Metrics
text:
QC Decisions Should Be Tested
QC filtering is a hypothesis.
Before applying thresholds, test whether:

High percent_mt cells cluster together
They are enriched in a specific batch
They align with a specific cell type

If filtering removes a coherent biological signal, it may be inappropriate.
QC is not about cleaning data until it looks nice.
It is about controlling technical noise while preserving biological structure.

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

Normalized counts
Log-transformed expression
Selected highly variable genes
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
Load Data and Prepare Matrix

source("scripts/R/cdi-plot-theme.R")

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

counts <- read.csv("data/demo-counts.csv", row.names = 1)
metadata <- read.csv("data/demo-metadata.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

library_size <- colSums(counts)
norm_counts <- sweep(counts, 2, library_size, "/") * 10000
log_counts <- log1p(norm_counts)

gene_vars  <- apply(log_counts, 1, var)
var_order <- order(gene_vars, decreasing = TRUE)
variable_genes <- rownames(log_counts)[var_order[1:200]]

mat <- t(log_counts[variable_genes, ])
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

pca <- prcomp(mat, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pc_df <- data.frame(
  cell_id = metadata$cell_id,
  PC1 = pca$x[,1],
  PC2 = pca$x[,2],
  percent_mt = metadata$percent_mt,
  batch = metadata$batch
)
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
PCA Colored by Mitochondrial Percentage

ggplot(pc_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = percent_mt)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "PCA colored by mitochondrial percentage",
    subtitle = "Technical structure may align with high percent_mt",
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()









Interpretation
Technical structure is driving separation.
PC1 is strongly aligned with mitochondrial percentage. This indicates that the dominant axis of variation is not purely biological.
Cells with high percent_mt are separating in reduced space, suggesting:

Technical stress
Apoptotic or dying cells
Capture inefficiency

If clustering were performed without QC awareness, this axis could be mistaken for a biological subtype.
In single-cell analysis, the first question after PCA is not:
“What cell type is this?”
It is:
“Is this biology, or is this technical structure?”
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
PCA Colored by Batch

ggplot(pc_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = batch)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA colored by batch",
    subtitle = "Batch-driven separation indicates technical variation",
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()









Interpretation
Batch does not dominate structure.
Batches are intermingled within clusters. There is no strong batch-specific axis.
This suggests:

Minimal batch effect
Reduced risk of confounding

Here, mitochondrial QC signal is stronger than batch signal.
That distinction matters.
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
Clustering (K-means Example)
Clustering assigns cells to algorithmic groups. Clusters are not automatically cell types.

set.seed(123)
kmeans_res <- kmeans(pc_df[, c("PC1", "PC2")], centers = 3)

pc_df$cluster <- as.factor(kmeans_res$cluster)
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
PCA with Cluster Labels

ggplot(pc_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA with cluster assignments",
    subtitle = "Clusters reflect structure in reduced space",
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()









Interpretation
One cluster is likely QC-driven.
The clustering algorithm did not discover biology. It discovered structure.
One cluster corresponds closely to the high percent_mt region, suggesting:

Stressed cells
Low-quality cells
A technical axis captured by PCA

The other clusters are more biologically plausible populations.
Dimensionality reduction and clustering do not create meaning. They reveal structure. Interpretation assigns meaning.
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
QC Check: percent_mt by Cluster
This plot tests whether mitochondrial percentage differs systematically across clusters.

ggplot(pc_df, aes(x = cluster, y = percent_mt)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.9, outlier.alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Mitochondrial percentage by cluster",
    subtitle = "Large shifts indicate clusters may be QC-driven",
    x = "Cluster",
    y = "percent_mt"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()









Interpretation
If one cluster has substantially higher percent_mt, it is a warning signal.
It suggests the cluster may reflect:

Cell stress
Low-quality capture
Technical separation

This does not force filtering. It forces calibration.
crumbs: 5  Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering

title: Lesson 4: Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering
text:
Structural Calibration Before Biological Annotation
Before labeling clusters as biological identities, rule out:

QC-driven clusters
Mitochondrial bias
Library size effects
Batch artifacts

In this dataset:

One cluster is likely technical.
Two clusters are biologically plausible.

That calibration step prevents false biological narratives.

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
From Clusters to Markers
Clustering groups cells based on expression similarity.
Marker analysis asks:
Which genes distinguish one cluster from the others?
Clusters are algorithmic. Markers provide biological evidence.
Marker detection is still a statistical model, not proof of identity.
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
Load Data and Recreate Objects

source("scripts/R/cdi-plot-theme.R")

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

# Read counts as numeric matrix (avoid character columns)
counts_df <- read.csv("data/demo-counts.csv", check.names = FALSE)
rownames(counts_df) <- counts_df[, 1]
counts_df <- counts_df[, -1, drop = FALSE]
counts <- as.matrix(counts_df)
storage.mode(counts) <- "numeric"

metadata <- read.csv("data/demo-metadata.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Normalize + log transform
library_size <- colSums(counts)
norm_counts <- sweep(counts, 2, library_size, "/") * 10000
log_counts <- log1p(norm_counts)

# Variable genes
gene_vars <- apply(log_counts, 1, var)
var_order <- order(gene_vars, decreasing = TRUE)
variable_genes <- rownames(log_counts)[var_order[1:200]]

# PCA for clustering
mat <- t(log_counts[variable_genes, ])
pca <- prcomp(mat, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pc_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pca$x[, 1],
  PC2 = pca$x[, 2]
)

set.seed(123)
kmeans_res <- kmeans(pc_df[, c("PC1", "PC2")], centers = 3)
clusters <- as.factor(kmeans_res$cluster)
table(clusters)

clusters
  1   2   3 
100 100 100
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
Simple Marker Detection (Cluster 1 vs Others)
For teaching, we use a per-gene two-sample t-test on log-normalized expression.
In real analyses, you should use models designed for single-cell data and account for confounding, library size, and zero inflation.

cluster_id <- "1"

group1 <- which(clusters == cluster_id)
group2 <- which(clusters != cluster_id)

marker_results <- data.frame(
  gene = rownames(log_counts),
  logFC = NA_real_,
  pvalue = NA_real_
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(log_counts))) {
  g1 <- as.numeric(log_counts[i, group1])
  g2 <- as.numeric(log_counts[i, group2])

  # Effect size (mean difference)
  marker_results$logFC[i] <- mean(g1, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(g2, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Some genes can be nearly constant; t.test may warn. We treat failures as NA.
  tt <- tryCatch(
    suppressWarnings(t.test(g1, g2)),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  marker_results$pvalue[i] <- if (is.null(tt)) NA_real_ else tt$p.value
}

marker_results$padj <- p.adjust(marker_results$pvalue, method = "BH")

# Define "significant" markers for visualization
marker_results$significant <- !is.na(marker_results$padj) & marker_results$padj < 0.05
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
Volcano Plot

volcano_df <- marker_results %>%
  mutate(neglog10_padj = -log10(padj))

sig_cutoff <- -log10(0.05)

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x = logFC, y = neglog10_padj)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = significant), alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "#036281")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sig_cutoff, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Marker gene volcano plot (Cluster 1)",
    subtitle = "Significant genes highlighted after multiple testing correction",
    x = "Mean difference in log expression (Cluster 1 minus others)",
    y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)"
  ) +
  cdi_theme()









Interpretation
This volcano plot shows three regimes:

Central cloud near logFC = 0
Genes with minimal difference between clusters. These form the null background.
Right tail (positive logFC, high significance)
Genes strongly higher in Cluster 1. Large effect sizes align with strong evidence.
Left tail (negative logFC)
Genes depleted in Cluster 1 relative to others.

What is striking here is not only statistical significance.
It is structural coherence.
The most significant genes are also those with large effect sizes. That alignment suggests Cluster 1 is genuinely distinct in expression space.
However, this does not yet prove biological identity. It confirms expression differentiation.
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
section: Statistical Strength Does Not Equal Biological Identity
text:
Statistical Strength Does Not Equal Biological Identity
This plot confirms:

Cluster 1 is transcriptionally distinct
The separation is not subtle
The signal survives multiple testing correction

But this does not tell us:

Whether this cluster represents a known cell type
Whether it reflects activation state
Whether it reflects stress
Whether it is a QC artifact

Remember from Lesson 4:
One cluster aligned with high percent_mt.
If this volcano plot corresponds to that cluster, we may be detecting stress-response genes.
Strong signal does not guarantee meaningful biology.
It guarantees difference.

crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
Critical Distinction
Clustering answers:
Which cells group together?
Marker analysis answers:
Which genes differentiate those groups?
Annotation answers:
What biological identity best explains those genes?
These are three separate steps.
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline

title: Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
text:
Annotation Is a Hypothesis
Even strong markers:

May reflect activation state rather than cell type
May be influenced by QC structure
May reflect stress responses

Annotation should be framed as:
“Cluster 1 is consistent with X-like cells based on its marker profile.”
Not:
“Cluster 1 is definitively X.”
crumbs: 6  Lesson 5: Marker Genes and Annotation Discipline
